messages.subject: Tomorrow: Tidyverse talk + work session
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I will give a talk at our weekly meeting tomorrow on the "tidyverse" (formerly "Hadleyverse"), which is about 20 R packages that work together to make most of what you do in R easier, faster, and less bug-prone. If you're new to R, come: the tidyverse syntax is less obtuse than base R and the consistency is refreshing. If you already use a few tidyverse packages like ggplot2 or dplyr, come: learn about additional tools that fit in your existing pipelines to make your work easier. And if you program with lists and don't know purrr yet, come: I just learned it and am quite excited about it -- convenient map-reduce functions, type-stable try and unlist, list-columns in data frames, and more. I'll walk through what each of these packages does, explain why you might want to use it, and demo its functionality and advantages over the base R alternatives. I will also demo the new R Notebooks, which is a nice way to build a dynamic document chunk by chunk.

We will start at 1:10pm, the talk will probably go to about 2:00, and we will have the usual work session after. In person in Wickson 2124, or if you can't make it, stream live and chat in your questions here <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_rPhSAVhs1A>. You can download the talk source materials here <https://github.com/michaellevy/tidyverse_talk>, sometime before 1pm tomorrow :).

See you tomorrow,

Michael

messages.subject: map() vs. lapply()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Yesterday, during the tidyverse talk, Michael showed the speed advantage of the map function vs the lapply function:

df = data_frame(fun = rep(c(lapply, map), 2),
                n = rep(c(1e5, 1e7), each = 2),
                comp_time = map2(fun, n, ~system.time(.x(1:.y, sqrt))))
df$comp_time
## [[1]]
##    user  system elapsed
##   0.042   0.003   0.046
##
## [[2]]
##    user  system elapsed
##   0.055   0.001   0.059
##
## [[3]]
##    user  system elapsed
##  12.366   0.218  12.612
##
## [[4]]
##    user  system elapsed
##   8.572   0.117   8.742

It seemed strange to me, since both call out to C and should be very fast. I suspected the culprit was wrapping the functions inside a tidyverse function. For comparison, I ran the tests from the presentation, then each test independently.

> df = data_frame(fun = rep(c(lapply, map), 2),
+                 n = rep(c(1e5, 1e7), each = 2),
+                 comp_time = map2(fun, n, ~system.time(.x(1:.y, sqrt))))

>df$comp_time
[[1]]
   user  system elapsed
  0.034   0.006   0.040

[[2]]
   user  system elapsed
  0.040   0.000   0.041

[[3]]
   user  system elapsed
 13.297   0.146  13.445

[[4]]
   user  system elapsed
  8.963   0.193   9.159

>system.time(lapply(1:1e5, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
  0.037   0.000   0.035
>system.time(map(1:1e5, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
  0.040   0.000   0.041
>system.time(lapply(1:1e7, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
  7.400   0.040   7.439
>system.time(map(1:1e7, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
  6.907   0.123   7.032

Looks like they are about even when not wrapped in a call to map2, with map() a hair faster for larger vectors.

Then for fun, I pre-allocated the large vector:

> x = 1:1e7
> system.time(lapply(x, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
  7.320   0.010   7.335
> system.time(map(x, sqrt))
   user  system elapsed
   7.69    0.00    7.69

Lapply comes out a hair ahead with the pre-allocated vector.

Lastly, both vs. a vectorized call:

> system.time(sqrt(x))
   user  system elapsed
  0.040   0.000   0.038

Short story:
 - benchmarking is tough
 - lapply and map are probably equally fast.
 - figuring out vectorized function calls in R is well worth it.

Hope someone finds this useful.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: map() vs. lapply()
messages.body_plain:
Interesting. Benchmarking can indeed be tricky, in part because the measurements are noisy. And as we discussed yesterday, for almost everyone, the time spent coding easily eclipses execution difference. For example, I just spent more time digging into this than I am likely to ever make up from what I learned. :)

I’ll say I definitely agree that finding ways to do vectorizable things with vectorized functions is important. Learning how to do that is a big part of learning to “think in R”. Duncan’s car-moving exercise (here <http://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/s/4n1bu5efjwhwcqm/hw2.pdf?dl=0> if anyone wants an R challenge!) is a great example of that. I don’t see the tidyverse functions moving learners away from vectorization, but I’d like to hear if others disagree.

To these benchmarks. I just tested five common tasks in base vs tidyverse, each replicated 10 times on data.frames with 1e5, 1e6, or 1e7 rows. Here are the results (means over ten replicates), followed by the code.

library(tidyverse)

reps = 10
dir.create("temp")

ns = c(n100000 = 1e5, n1000000 = 1e6, n10000000 = 1e7)
rats =
  lapply(ns, function(n) {
    d = data.frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))

    tidy = c(
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        data_frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        filter(d, y > 0)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        mutate(d, z = x * y)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        map(d$x, `^`, -2:2)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        write_csv(d, "temp/temp.csv")
      }))[3, ])
    )

    base = c(
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        data.frame(x = 1:n, y = rnorm(n))
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        d[d$y > 0, ]
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        d$x * d$y
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        lapply(d$x, `^`, -2:2)
      }))[3, ]),
      mean(replicate(reps, system.time({
        write.csv(d, "temp/temp.csv")
      }))[3, ])
    )

    return(list(tidy = tidy, base = base))
  })

map_df(rats, ~ log(.$tidy / .$base, base = 2)) %>%
  data.frame(fun = c("make-df", "subset-rows", "make-column", "lapply/map", "write-csv")) %>%
  gather(rows, tidy_base, -fun) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fun, y = tidy_base, color = rows)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "",
                     breaks = -2:2, labels = c("4x\ntidyverse faster", "2x", "even", "2x", "4x\nbase faster")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 18) +
  xlab("")
​

--
Michael Levy
970-426-5389

My 2c:

I cannot talk extensively about the ease of teaching the tidyverse vs. base beyond the observation that many people who learn the tidyverse are not actually learning R so much as they are stringing together commands through trial and error until they find something that appears to work. Certainly not all, but many lack much understanding about what they are doing.

I personally find the tidyverse way of writing code much more difficult to read. Some of the non-standard evaluation and non-standard scoping only adds to this. As for convenience, there is nothing in the tidyverse that I cannot do in base R, and often with much less code written.

However, my biggest concern with the tidyverse is how much it limits R. For example, tidy data might be great for most use cases, but sometimes data are best arranged wide, in lists of lists, or in some other non-tidy format (and sometimes you don't have a choice). Knowing the basics of indexing and subsetting in base R allows you to tackle data in just about any format. From what I have seen, the same cannot be said for the tidyverse.

By analogy, this reminds me of my experience prior to UCD. I built furniture. Sure, you can build a table with some fancy jig-o-matic, but you need specialized tools and faith in the jig-maker. At the end of the day all you know how to build is the table the jig-maker designed. Learn the fundamentals of joinery, and you can build just about anything with just a handful of basic tools. Will you have a table faster with the jig? Probably. Can you build anything else? Probably not.

Matt

You are probably correct that many people will never get to that point and I freely admit that my experience may be atypical, but I think it is good for people to be aware of. Here is an example of a computationally reproducible paper I wrote a few years back:

https://github.com/csu-hmc/perturbed-data-paper

The source for the manuscript and the source to create the figures are in the repository. After cloning the repo, you can run a simple make command to build the paper. You have to install the software dependencies first (the main package dependency is versioned and hosted on a package repository), then you can simply call make to download the raw data, run analysis, and generate the paper in one command. In the caption of each figure or table I reference the script that generates that item.

I've had a number of people build the paper on their computer to ensure it worked cross-platform. The main hassle is installing the software, which I'd alleviate in the future with a conda environment or docker image.

This is one of many ways you could can do this.
